scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is asking if it's morally acceptable for someone to just be themselves, even if it's causing friction in a new cultural environment. Let me break this down.

First, the person is a 23-year-old British man who moved to the US for work. He's been there for three months. He's always been himself, with a very British sense of humor, which includes dark jokes and being offensive in a friendly way. He's found that in the US, people are much nicer and more politically correct, which he finds fake and hard to deal with. He's tried toning down his personality but still feels like he doesn't fit in. Some people have called him an asshole (AH) because of his behavior, while others, like his flatmates, appreciate his personality.

He's feeling stuck because he doesn't want to change who he is, but he's struggling to fit in. He's considering whether he's an asshole for just being himself.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for him to continue being himself, even if it leads to others labeling him as an asshole?

I think the key points here are about cultural adaptation, authenticity, and the impact of one's behavior on others. On one hand, being true to oneself is a positive trait. It's important to stay authentic and not change who you are just to fit in. On the other hand, when moving to a new culture, there's an expectation to adapt to some extent to build relationships and integrate into the community.

In this case, the person has already made some adjustments, like toning down his humor, but he's still facing pushback. Some people find him off-putting, while others appreciate his honesty. The fact that he's had to adjust at all shows that he's aware of cultural differences and is making an effort to adapt, which is a positive step.

However, the problem arises when his behavior is causing others to feel uncomfortable or to label him negatively. While it's not wrong to be yourself, it's also important to consider the impact of your actions on others. If his humor or personality is consistently causing friction or making others feel disrespected, then it might be crossing a line into being inconsiderate or hurtful, even if it's unintentional.

But in this scenario, the person is clearly trying to adapt and is only toning down his behavior, not completely changing it. He's also expressing that he's a caring and loyal person, which are positive traits. The fact that some people appreciate him while others don't is a common experience in cultural adaptation. It's possible that he's in a situation where his personality doesn't align with the majority, but that doesn't necessarily make him an asshole.

So, considering all this, I think the action of staying true to oneself, even in the face of cultural differences, is morally acceptable. It's important to maintain authenticity, and while adapting to a new culture is necessary, it doesn't mean losing one's identity. The person is making an effort to adjust, which shows consideration, even if he's still struggling to fit in.
